The tail-current constraint is

\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1 .
\]

Also,

\[
V_{\text{out}}=V_{DD}-R_D I_{D2}.
\]

For matched devices and \(V_{\text{in}}=V_b\),

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_1}{2},
\]

and hence

\[
V_{\text{out},Q}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1R_D}{2}.
\]

The common-source voltage is

\[
V_X=V_{\text{in}}-V_{GS1}=V_b-V_{GS2}.
\]

As \(V_{\text{in}}\) rises above \(V_b\), \(M_1\) takes more of the tail current, \(M_2\) takes less, and \(V_{\text{out}}\) rises. Thus, the overall voltage gain is noninverting.

---

## Small-signal gain

Let \(v_x\), \(v_{\text{in}}\), and \(v_b\) be small-signal voltages. Since the ideal tail source supplies no incremental current,

\[
g_{m1}(v_{\text{in}}-v_x)+g_{m2}(v_b-v_x)=0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
v_x=
\frac{g_{m1}v_{\text{in}}+g_{m2}v_b}
{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}.
\]

The small-signal drain current of \(M_2\) is

\[
i_{d2}=g_{m2}(v_b-v_x)
=
-\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}
(v_{\text{in}}-v_b).
\]

Since

\[
v_{\text{out}}=-R_D i_{d2},
\]

the differential-to-single-ended voltage gain is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}-v_b}
=
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
}
\]

If \(V_b\) is an ideal dc bias, then \(v_b=0\), giving

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
}
\]

For matched transistors, \(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\),

\[
\boxed{
v_x=\frac{v_{\text{in}}}{2},
\qquad
A_v=\frac{g_mR_D}{2}.
}
\]

Thus, it is incorrect to assume that the source follower has unity gain and conclude that the total gain is \(g_mR_D\). The common-gate input presents approximately \(1/g_{m2}\) to the source follower, reducing its gain.

---

## Interpretation as two cascaded stages

- \(M_1\) has approximate source-follower output resistance

\[
R_{\text{out},M1}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}}.
\]

- Looking into the source of the common-gate device,

\[
R_{\text{in},M2}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{1/g_{m2}}{1/g_{m1}+1/g_{m2}}
=
\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}.
\]

The common-gate gain is approximately

\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_x}\approx +g_{m2}R_D,
\]

and their product gives the result above.

- Input resistance at \(V_{\text{in}}\): ideally infinite, since it is a MOS gate.
- Output resistance: approximately \(R_D\) if \(r_o\) is neglected.
- With a load \(R_L\), replace \(R_D\) by \(R_D\parallel R_L\).
- If the tail source has finite small-signal resistance \(r_{I1}\),

\[
A_v \approx
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_D}
{g_{m1}+g_{m2}+1/r_{I1}}.
\]

Finally, saturation must be maintained:

\[
V_{DD}-V_X \ge V_{OV1},
\qquad
V_{\text{out}}-V_X \ge V_{OV2}.
\]

For large positive \(V_{\text{in}}-V_b\), \(M_2\) turns off and \(V_{\text{out}}\to V_{DD}\). For large negative \(V_{\text{in}}-V_b\), \(M_2\) carries nearly all of \(I_1\), so ideally \(V_{\text{out}}\to V_{DD}-I_1R_D\), subject to the saturation constraint.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

Although no physical inductor is shown, \(M_1\)’s intrinsic \(C_{gs1}\) is part of an active feedback path.

\[
\frac{v_g}{R_S}+sC_{gs1}(v_g-v_o)=0,
\]

so

\[
v_o-v_g=\frac{v_o}{1+sR_SC_{gs1}}.
\]

The test current drawn at the output is approximately

\[
i_t=(g_{m1}+sC_{gs1})(v_o-v_g),
\]

giving

\[
Z_\text{out}\simeq
\frac{1+sR_SC_{gs1}}{g_{m1}+sC_{gs1}}
=
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
\frac{1+sR_SC_{gs1}}
{1+sC_{gs1}/g_{m1}}.
\]

This impedance has a zero at

\[
\omega_z=\frac{1}{R_SC_{gs1}}
\]

and a pole at

\[
\omega_p=\frac{g_{m1}}{C_{gs1}}.
\]

If

\[
g_{m1}R_S>1,
\]

the zero occurs before the pole, producing positive phase in \(Z_\text{out}\), i.e., inductive behavior. Its low-frequency expansion is

\[
Z_\text{out}\approx
\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
+s\,\frac{C_{gs1}(g_{m1}R_S-1)}{g_{m1}^2}.
\]

Thus the second term acts like \(sL\). For \(g_{m1}R_S\gg 1\),

\[
L_\text{eff}\approx \frac{R_SC_{gs1}}{g_{m1}}.
\]

Physically, a change in \(V_\text{out}\) drives current through \(C_{gs1}\) and \(R_S\), creating a delayed/phase-shifted gate voltage. The resulting \(g_m\) current opposes the normal capacitive current at the output. Since \(M_1\) is biased and active, this capacitive feedback can synthesize an apparent inductance.

\[

M_1 & X & V_{\text{out}} & 0\\

\[
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=
I_{D1}(V_{GS1}=V_X,\;V_{DS1}=V_{\text{out}})
\]

and

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=
I_{D2}(V_{GS2}=V_{\text{out}},\;V_{DS2}=V_X).

\[

\[

=

\qquad

4. Less current is removed from node \(X\).

\[

\;\rightarrow\;
V_{\text{out}}\downarrow
\;\rightarrow\;
I_{D2}\downarrow
\;\rightarrow\;
V_X\uparrow.
\]

\[

=
\left(g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_L\right)v_x.

\[

=
\frac{v_x}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
\frac{1}
{g_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_L}.

=

\frac{r_{o2}}{1-T}

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
Let \(v_s\) denote the source node of \(M_1\) (the input summing node), and assume \(V_b\) and \(V_{DD}\) are ac grounds. Both MOSFETs are assumed to be in saturation.

- \(M_1\) is a common-gate stage.
- \(M_2\) is a common-source stage.
- \(R_F\) feeds a sampled output voltage back as a current into the input node.

Thus, this is a **shunt-shunt negative-feedback transimpedance amplifier**.

## Forward-path gain

Let \(i_e\) be the net current entering the source of \(M_1\). Neglecting \(r_o\),

\[
v_s \simeq \frac{i_e}{g_{m1}}
\]

and the common-gate stage gives

\[
v_X=g_{m1}R_{D1}v_s=R_{D1}i_e.
\]

The second stage then produces

\[
v_{out}=-g_{m2}R_{D2}v_X.
\]

Hence the forward transimpedance is

\[
v_{out}=-Z_A i_e,
\qquad
Z_A=g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}.
\]

The minus sign arises because \(M_2\) is a common-source stage.

## Feedback action

Taking \(i_{RF}\) as positive in the direction shown, from the output toward the input,

\[
i_{RF}\simeq \frac{v_{out}}{R_F}.
\]

At the input summing node,

\[
i_e=i_{in}+i_{RF}.
\]

Since \(v_{out}=-Z_Ai_e\),

\[
i_e=i_{in}-\frac{Z_A}{R_F}i_e.
\]

Therefore,

\[
i_e=\frac{i_{in}}{1+T},
\]

where the loop-gain magnitude is

\[
\boxed{T=\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}}.
\]

The closed-loop transimpedance is then

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
=
-\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}
{1+\dfrac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}}
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
=
-R_F\frac{T}{1+T}.
}
\]

For a large loop gain, \(T\gg 1\),

\[
\boxed{v_{out}\simeq -R_F i_{in}.}
\]

Thus the circuit behaves as an inverting transimpedance amplifier whose gain is set primarily by \(R_F\), rather than by transistor parameters.

For a positive incremental \(i_{in}\), the output moves negative. Consequently, the actual resistor current flows from the input node toward the output, opposing the input-current change. This confirms that the feedback is negative.

## Input and output resistance

Ignoring loading by \(R_F\), the open-loop input resistance is approximately

\[
R_{in,0}\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m1}}.
\]

Shunt mixing reduces it by the loop gain:

\[
\boxed{
R_{in,\mathrm{cl}}\simeq
\frac{1/g_{m1}}{1+T}.
}
\]

Likewise, voltage sampling at the output reduces output resistance approximately as

\[
\boxed{
R_{out,\mathrm{cl}}\simeq
\frac{R_{D2}}{1+T}.
}
\]

These are the usual shunt-shunt feedback effects: both input and output resistance decrease.

## More exact low-frequency result

If the loading of \(R_F\) is retained, with \(r_o\to\infty\) and no external output load,

\[
v_X=g_{m1}R_{D1}v_s,
\]

\[
i_{in}=g_{m1}v_s+\frac{v_s-v_{out}}{R_F},
\]

\[
\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+g_{m2}v_X+
\frac{v_{out}-v_s}{R_F}=0.
\]

Solving gives

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
=
\frac{
R_{D2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}R_F
}{
1+g_{m1}(R_F+R_{D2})
+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}
}.
}
\]

For sufficiently large gain, this again approaches \(-R_F\).

Finally, the dc bias must keep both devices in saturation:

\[
V_X-V_S \ge V_{OV1},
\qquad
V_{out}\ge V_{OV2}.
\]

The relation \(v_{out}\simeq -R_F i_{in}\) is an incremental small-signal result about that bias point.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
Let \(V_x\) denote the lower summing node. Using the device arrows in the figure,

\[
\begin{aligned}
M_1 &: \text{NMOS common-gate device},\quad D=V_{\text{out}},\ G=V_b,\ S=V_x,\\
M_2 &: \text{PMOS feedback device},\quad S=V_{DD},\ G=V_{\text{out}},\ D=V_x.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let the unlabelled downward current source at \(V_x\) be \(I_B\).

## DC operation

Assume both MOSFETs are in saturation, channel-length modulation is neglected, and the output is not externally dc-loaded.

At the output node, the current supplied by \(I_1\) must flow through \(M_1\):

\[
I_{D1}=I_1.
\]

Thus \(M_1\) establishes the dc voltage at the summing node:

\[
I_1=\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_b-V_x-V_{TN})^2
\]

or

\[
V_x=V_b-V_{TN}-\sqrt{\frac{2I_1}{\beta_n}}.
\]

At node \(V_x\), KCL gives

\[
I_B=I_{\text{in}}+I_{D1}+I_{D2},
\]

so

\[
I_{D2}=I_B-I_1-I_{\text{in}}.
\]

For PMOS \(M_2\),

\[
I_{D2}=
\frac{\beta_p}{2}
\left(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}-\left|V_{TP}\right|\right)^2.
\]

Therefore, the large-signal current-to-voltage characteristic is

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{out}}
=
V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|
-\sqrt{\frac{2\left(I_B-I_1-I_{\text{in}}\right)}{\beta_p}}
}
\]

provided \(M_2\) remains on and saturated.

An increase in \(I_{\text{in}}\) decreases the current required from \(M_2\), so \(V_{\text{out}}\) must rise to reduce \(M_2\)'s \(V_{SG}\).

---

## Small-signal behavior

For \(M_2\),

\[
\Delta I_{D2}=-g_{m2}\Delta V_{\text{out}}.
\]

Since \(I_B\) and \(I_1\) are fixed ideally,

\[
\Delta I_{\text{in}}+\Delta I_{D2}=0.
\]

Hence,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{\Delta V_{\text{out}}}{\Delta I_{\text{in}}}
\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m2}}
}
\]

where

\[
g_{m2}
=
\beta_p\left(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}-|V_{TP}|\right)
=
\frac{2I_{D2}}{V_{OV2}}.
\]

Thus the circuit is a current-to-voltage converter whose small-signal transimpedance is set mainly by the transconductance of the PMOS feedback transistor \(M_2\).

The polarity is positive:

\[
I_{\text{in}}\uparrow
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
I_{D2}\downarrow
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
V_{\text{out}}\uparrow.
\]

---

## Feedback interpretation

\(M_2\) senses \(V_{\text{out}}\) and feeds a current back to the input summing node:

\[
i_f \simeq g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}.
\]

It is shunt-shunt negative feedback:

- input currents are summed at \(V_x\);
- output voltage is sensed at the gate of \(M_2\);
- a rise in \(V_{\text{out}}\) reduces PMOS current into \(V_x\), opposing an increase in \(I_{\text{in}}\).

If the output has a finite small-signal resistance \(R_o\), including the finite output resistance of \(I_1\), \(M_1\), and any load, then approximately

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
\simeq
\frac{R_o}{1+g_{m2}R_o}
}
\]

with loop gain

\[
T\simeq g_{m2}R_o.
\]

For strong feedback, \(g_{m2}R_o\gg 1\),

\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
\]

The feedback also lowers the input resistance approximately to

\[
R_{\text{in}}
\simeq
\frac{1}{g_{m1}(1+g_{m2}R_o)}.
\]

---

## Operating-range conditions

For the preceding equations to hold:

\[
I_B-I_1-I_{\text{in}}>0
\]

so that \(M_2\) remains on, and approximately

\[
V_{\text{out}}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|
\]

for \(M_2\) to conduct,

\[
V_x\leq V_{\text{out}}+|V_{TP}|
\]

for \(M_2\) saturation, and

\[
V_{\text{out}}\geq V_b-V_{TN}
\]

for \(M_1\) saturation.

Thus, \(I_1\), \(I_B\), and \(V_b\) establish the bias point, while \(M_2\) sets the principal small-signal current-to-voltage gain.

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 5 fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No—assuming the capacitors are finite and the inverters can supply the required charging/discharging current.

This is a three-stage ring oscillator. Increasing each load capacitance increases each inverter’s propagation delay, so the oscillation becomes slower. Roughly,

\[
t_{pd}\approx 0.69R_{\text{out}}C_L,
\qquad
T\approx 6t_{pd},
\]

for identical stages, so

\[
f \propto \frac{1}{C_L}.
\]

Thus, arbitrarily large *finite* capacitors produce an arbitrarily low frequency and very slow startup, rather than a particular capacitance at which oscillation inherently stops.

In the literal limit \(C_L\to\infty\), the period tends to infinity and the frequency tends to zero; the node voltages cannot change in finite time, so that limiting circuit does not oscillate in the ordinary sense. Practical circuits may also appear to stop for very large capacitors because of leakage, limited output current, supply loading, or insufficient observation time.

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in Figure 8, consider the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,

From the dynamic charging and discharging of the three load capacitances, one

```text
RX ~= 1 / (3 f0 CL)
```

Somebody then argues that, because the circuit is oscillating, the path from
`VDD` to ground through the transistors is off for much of the cycle, so the
average resistance should be much higher than the MOS on-resistance or inverse
transconductance scale.

Do you agree with this argument?

answer.text:
No—at least not for the effective, average supply resistance represented by

\[
R_X \simeq \frac{1}{3f_0C_L}.
\]

Each of the three internal nodes undergoes one low-to-high transition per oscillation period. The supply therefore delivers approximately

\[
Q_{\text{cycle}} \simeq 3C_LV_{DD}
\]

per cycle, so

\[
\overline{I}_{DD}\simeq 3f_0C_LV_{DD},
\qquad
P\simeq 3f_0C_LV_{DD}^2.
\]

Thus the power-equivalent resistance is

\[
R_X=\frac{V_{DD}}{\overline{I}_{DD}}
 \simeq \frac{1}{3f_0C_L}.
\]

For a three-stage ring oscillator, using the usual propagation-delay relation,

\[
T_0 \simeq 2(3)T_D=6T_D,
\qquad f_0\simeq \frac{1}{6T_D}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
R_X \simeq \frac{1}{3(1/6T_D)C_L}
      = \frac{2T_D}{C_L}.
\]

Now write the inverter delay in a simple effective-resistance form:

\[
T_D \simeq kR_{\rm drv}C_L,
\]

where \(k\) is an order-one waveform-dependent factor. Then

\[
R_X \simeq 2kR_{\rm drv}.
\]

For example, with the usual RC 50%-delay estimate \(k\simeq\ln 2\),

\[
R_X \simeq 1.4R_{\rm drv}.
\]

Likewise, if \(T_D\sim C_L/g_m\), then

\[
R_X\sim \frac{2}{g_m}.
\]

So \(R_X\) is of the same order as the inverter’s effective on-resistance or inverse transconductance, perhaps differing by a factor of order unity—not orders of magnitude larger merely because the devices are off part of the cycle.

The key point is that a direct simultaneous \(V_{DD}\)-to-ground transistor path is not required. During a rising transition, the supply charges \(C_L\) through the pMOS device; during a falling transition, the stored energy is dissipated through the nMOS device to ground. From the supply's averaged viewpoint, this is a switched-capacitor loss.

A stopped CMOS ring does indeed have a very large DC resistance, aside from leakage. But that is a different quantity from the dynamic, oscillating supply resistance \(R_X\). Strictly, the supply current is pulsed and time-varying, so \(R_X\) is an averaged/power-equivalent resistance rather than a literal fixed resistor.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
Let \(Q\) be the output of the rightmost inverter (the node fed back to the left), and let \(X\) be the output of \(\mathrm{Inv}_1\).

- **When \(CK=1\):**  
  The \(CK\)-controlled switch is on and the \(\overline{CK}\)-controlled switch is off.  
  Thus the first dynamic latch is transparent:

  \[
  X=\overline{Q}.
  \]

  The right-hand latch is isolated, so \(Q\) remains at its previously stored value.

- **When \(CK=0\) (\(\overline{CK}=1\)):**  
  The first switch opens, retaining the value sampled in the first latch, while the second switch closes.  
  The two inverters on the right have overall noninverting polarity, so they transfer \(X\) to \(Q\):

  \[
  Q_{\text{next}}=X.
  \]

Combining the two phases gives

\[
Q_{\text{next}}=\overline{Q}.
\]

Therefore, the feedback state complements once per clock cycle. For example,

\[
0 \rightarrow 1 \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow 1 \rightarrow \cdots
\]

at successive active clock edges. Hence the circuit is a **dynamic toggle flip-flop**, or equivalently a **divide-by-two circuit**:

\[
f_Q=\frac{f_{CK}}{2}.
\]

With the switch convention shown, \(Q\) changes on the falling edge of \(CK\); the complementary node \(X\) updates during the high phase.

Because this is a dynamic circuit, its operation depends on charge stored on the isolated latch nodes. It requires:

- sufficiently fast clocking to overcome leakage,
- adequate time in each clock phase for propagation,
- nonoverlapping clock phases.

If both switches are on simultaneously, all three inverters form an odd-inversion feedback loop, which can race or oscillate rather than divide reliably.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
The 50-\(\Omega\) requirement is imposed by the **feedback loop**, not by simply choosing \(R_F=50~\Omega\).

Let \(v_g\) be the common gate voltage of \(M_1\) and \(M_2\), and let

\[
A=-\frac{v_o}{v_g}>0
\]

be the magnitude of the inverter voltage gain at the frequency of interest. Neglecting gate current and treating \(C_1\) as an RF short,

\[
i_{\rm in}=\frac{v_g-v_o}{R_F}
          =\frac{(1+A)v_g}{R_F}.
\]

Hence,

\[
R_{\rm in}=\frac{R_F}{1+A}.
\]

Therefore, to maintain a 50-\(\Omega\) input resistance,

\[
\boxed{R_F=50(1+A)}.
\]

So \(R_F\) should be treated as a dependent design variable: whenever transistor sizes, bias current, or output loading change the gain, retune \(R_F\) to preserve \(R_{\rm in}=50~\Omega\).

Using \(G_m=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\) and an output resistance \(R_o\) before feedback, a more explicit small-signal result is

\[
R_{\rm in}=\frac{R_F+R_o}{1+G_mR_o},
\]

so the matching constraint becomes

\[
\boxed{R_F=50(1+G_mR_o)-R_o.}
\]

For \(R_F\gg R_o\), this reduces to the familiar approximation

\[
R_F\simeq 50(1+G_mR_o).
\]

A useful first-order noise-factor expression is

\[
F \simeq 1+
\frac{R_F}{R_S(1+A)^2}
+
\frac{\gamma_n g_{m1}+\gamma_p g_{m2}}
{R_S(g_{m1}+g_{m2})^2}
+\text{other noise terms},
\]

where \(R_S=50~\Omega\), and the other terms include induced gate noise, output/load noise, \(C_1\) loss, and parasitics. With the 50-\(\Omega\) constraint enforced,

\[
F \simeq 1+
\frac{1}{1+A}
+
\frac{\gamma_n g_{m1}+\gamma_p g_{m2}}
{50(g_{m1}+g_{m2})^2}
+\cdots .
\]

Thus, the design direction is:

- maximize the useful inverter gain \(A\), allowing a larger \(R_F\) while retaining \(R_{\rm in}=50~\Omega\);
- maximize noise-efficient total transconductance \(g_{m1}+g_{m2}\);
- include noise from both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\); \(M_2\) is not a noiseless load;
- at the operating frequency, constrain the full impedance to approximately
  \[
  Z_{\rm in}=50+j0~\Omega,
  \]
  not just its real part;
- optimize \(W_1\), \(W_2\), bias current, output loading, and \(R_F\) in a constrained AC/noise simulation, while also enforcing gain, bandwidth, power, linearity, and stability requirements.

With only the condition \(R_{\rm in}=50~\Omega\), there is no finite ideal optimum: increasing \(G_m\) and gain keeps reducing the dominant noise terms. The practical optimum is set by current consumption, device capacitance/\(f_T\), bandwidth, stability, and the transistor noise model.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Treat the LDO as an ideal dc supply plus a small noise voltage at the VCO supply node:

\[
V_{\text{out}}(t)=V_{\text{out,DC}}+v_n(t).
\]

First obtain the noise PSD actually present at the loaded VCO supply node:

\[
S_{v_n}(f)=|H_{\text{LDO},n\rightarrow \text{out}}(f)|^2S_{\text{th}}(f).
\]

If \(S_{\text{th}}\) is already the LDO output-referred voltage-noise PSD in \(\mathrm{V^2/Hz}\), then simply \(S_{v_n}=S_{\text{th}}\).

The needed VCO parameter is the **supply-pushing sensitivity**, not necessarily the normal tuning gain \(df_0/dV_{\text{cont}}\):

\[
K_{f,DD}=\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}\quad [\mathrm{Hz/V}],
\]

or equivalently,

\[
K_{\omega,DD}=2\pi K_{f,DD}.
\]

For low-offset supply noise, the supply perturbation produces frequency noise,

\[
\delta f(t)=K_{f,DD}v_n(t),
\]

and phase is the integral of frequency:

\[
S_{\phi,\text{LDO}}(\Delta f)
=
\left(\frac{K_{f,DD}}{\Delta f}\right)^2
S_{v_n}(\Delta f).
\]

Thus the single-sideband phase-noise contribution is

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L_{\text{LDO}}(\Delta f)
=
10\log_{10}
\left[
\frac{1}{2}
\left(\frac{K_{f,DD}}{\Delta f}\right)^2
S_{v_n}(\Delta f)
\right]
\quad \text{dBc/Hz}
}
\]

where the factor \(1/2\) is for the usual one-sided \(S_\phi\)-to-SSB-phase-noise convention.

More generally, define a supply-to-phase transfer function,

\[
H_{\phi,VDD}(f)=\frac{\Phi(f)}{V_{\text{out}}(f)}.
\]

Then,

\[
S_{\phi,\text{LDO}}(f)
=
|H_{\phi,VDD}(f)|^2S_{v_n}(f),
\qquad
\mathcal L(f)=10\log_{10}\!\left[\frac{S_\phi(f)}{2}\right].
\]

For an LC VCO, especially if LDO noise near \(f_0\), \(2f_0\), etc. can fold into close-in phase noise, obtain \(H_{\phi,VDD}\) with a periodic analysis such as PSS/PXF/PNoise or an ISF-based calculation. That captures AM-to-PM conversion, device nonlinearities, and harmonic mixing.

Finally, the LDO noise is applied largely as a common-mode disturbance to the two inductor center taps. An ideal perfectly symmetric VCO may reject it strongly, but mismatch, voltage-dependent capacitances, finite tail-source impedance, and AM-to-PM conversion make \(K_{f,DD}\) nonzero in practice. Add this contribution to the intrinsic VCO phase-noise PSD in linear units.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

\[
